entries.statement: A critical user journey has not been tested successfully end to end.
Authentication, authorization, administrative access, or tenant isolation has not been independently verified.
A known critical vulnerability or relevant known-exploited vulnerability remains unmitigated.
Production secrets, signing keys, credentials, tokens, or personal data have been exposed.
A destructive or irreversible data migration has not been rehearsed against representative data.
Backup restoration has not been demonstrated within the required recovery objectives.
Rollback or safe roll-forward has not been demonstrated.
Expected peak load, burst load, or dependency-failure behavior is unknown.
The release cannot meet its approved reliability objectives under expected operating conditions.
Monitoring cannot detect failure of critical user journeys.
No qualified person is available and authorized to respond during and immediately after launch.
Required incident-response, escalation, customer-communication, or breach-notification procedures do not exist.
A mandatory legal, privacy, payment, accessibility, safety, or contractual requirement is unmet.
The production artifact cannot be traced to reviewed source, dependencies, build process, tests, and approval.
An unsupported or end-of-life runtime, operating system, database, library, service, or protocol is required for operation.
Known data corruption, cross-user disclosure, cross-tenant access, duplicate charging, or irreversible financial risk remains possible without a tested control.
A single person, credential, machine, region, provider, or undocumented manual procedure is the only recovery path.
Evidence was collected before material changes that have not been retested.
A release blocker has been relabeled, suppressed, or accepted without an accountable risk owner.
The team cannot describe concrete stop, rollback, and incident-declaration criteria before deployment begins.
Assign a unique release identifier.
Record the exact source commit or commits.
Record the immutable application artifact digest.
Record every deployable service, worker, scheduled job, frontend bundle, and infrastructure component included.
Record database schema and migration versions.
Record production configuration versions.
Record feature flags and their intended launch states.
Record third-party service and API versions relied upon.
Record the intended production regions, accounts, projects, clusters, and domains.
Record the target deployment date and change window.
Record the previous known-good release and rollback artifact.
Freeze or formally track changes after the readiness evidence snapshot.
List every user-facing domain and subdomain.
List every API, webhook, callback, streaming connection, and machine interface.
List background workers, queues, scheduled tasks, batch processes, and administrative tools.
List databases, object stores, search indexes, caches, message brokers, analytics stores, and backup locations.
List external identity, payment, email, SMS, analytics, advertising, support, logging, CDN, and infrastructure providers.
List all user types, administrative roles, service accounts, and external actors.
List supported countries, languages, currencies, time zones, browsers, devices, and accessibility targets.
List all data classifications and regulated data handled.
List all excluded components and explain why they are outside the release assessment.
Identify every shared platform or dependency that can affect the app even though another team operates it.
The problem being solved and intended users are documented.
Release scope, non-goals, and deferred features are explicit.
Every feature has testable acceptance criteria.
Critical user journeys are ranked by business and user impact.
Critical journeys include onboarding, normal use, error recovery, account recovery, cancellation, and deletion where applicable.
Product behavior for unavailable dependencies and partial failure is specified.
Product behavior for empty, malformed, incomplete, stale, or conflicting data is specified.
User-visible terminology is consistent.
Pricing, entitlements, quotas, billing rules, and plan limits are unambiguous.
Cancellation, refund, reversal, dispute, and undo behavior is defined.
Expected customer support obligations are documented.
Service hours, maintenance expectations, SLOs, SLAs, and contractual commitments are aligned.
The launch does not make claims that the implemented product cannot substantiate.
Product management has accepted the final behavior of critical journeys.
Define measurable launch success criteria.
Define measurable launch failure and rollback criteria.
Define adoption, conversion, quality, reliability, support, and safety indicators.
Define the observation period before declaring the launch complete.
Define who has authority to pause, continue, expand, or roll back the launch.
Establish expected traffic and customer cohorts.
Establish whether the launch is internal, private, regional, percentage-based, invitation-only, or public.
Ensure marketing, sales, support, and operations use the same release date and scope.
Ensure help content, screenshots, pricing pages, documentation, and legal text match the released behavior.
Ensure customers are notified of breaking changes, downtime, migrations, or changed data use where required.
Every production service has a named business owner.
Every production service has a named engineering owner.
Every data set has an accountable data owner.
Every security-sensitive component has a security contact.
Every third-party integration has an owner.
Every operational dashboard, alert, and runbook has an owner.
Every scheduled job and background process has an owner.
Ownership remains valid during holidays, leave, and personnel changes.
Escalation paths include primary, secondary, management, security, privacy/legal, and provider escalation contacts.
Offboarding and role-change processes remove or adjust access promptly.
Classify confidentiality impact.
Classify integrity impact.
Classify availability impact.
Classify privacy impact.
Classify financial and fraud impact.
Classify physical, psychological, societal, and user-safety impact.
Classify regulatory and contractual impact.
Classify reputational and customer-trust impact.
Identify likely attackers, abusive users, insiders, compromised accounts, automated agents, and accidental failure sources.
Identify foreseeable misuse and abuse cases, not only intended use.
Maintain a release-specific risk register.
Give each risk an owner, likelihood, impact, treatment, evidence, and review date.
Record accepted residual risk and the person authorized to accept it.
Review high-impact assumptions with independent subject-matter experts.
Verify that launch scope remains inside the organization’s risk appetite.
Ensure risk exceptions cannot remain open indefinitely.
Ensure compensating controls are tested rather than merely described.
Map applicable security controls to a recognized verification standard.
Map applicable privacy controls to legal and organizational requirements.
Map accessibility requirements to the selected WCAG conformance target.
Map operational controls to SLO, incident, continuity, and recovery requirements.
Map contractual controls to customer, processor, provider, and partner agreements.
Identify conflicts between product requirements, legal requirements, and technical controls.
Document how conflicts were resolved and who approved the resolution.
Apply separation of duties to high-impact changes and approvals.
Periodically review whether the selected control level still matches the app’s risk.
Maintain an up-to-date system-context diagram.
Maintain component and deployment diagrams.
Maintain end-to-end data-flow diagrams.
Mark trust boundaries explicitly.
Mark Internet-facing and externally reachable interfaces.
Mark administrative and support interfaces.
Mark where authentication and authorization decisions occur.
Mark encryption and decryption boundaries.
Mark where sensitive data is collected, transformed, stored, cached, logged, exported, backed up, and deleted.
Mark all third-party data transfers.
Identify every stateful component.
Identify every asynchronous boundary and queue.
Identify common dependencies and shared failure domains.
Identify single points of failure.
Identify control-plane dependencies needed during incidents or recovery.
Identify circular and hidden dependency chains.
Document required consistency, ordering, durability, and freshness properties.
Document architectural invariants that must never be violated.
Document expected failure behavior for every critical dependency.
Record material architecture decisions and rejected alternatives.
Update diagrams whenever the release changes data flow, trust, topology, or dependencies.
Verify the documented architecture against the deployed environment rather than assuming documentation is accurate.
Perform a threat model for the actual release scope.
Include all trust boundaries, actors, entry points, data stores, and external systems.
Model spoofing and identity attacks.
Model unauthorized modification and integrity attacks.
Model information disclosure and privacy attacks.
Model denial of service and resource exhaustion.
Model privilege escalation.
Model repudiation and inadequate accountability.
Model business-logic abuse.
Model insider and compromised-administrator threats.
Model dependency and build-system compromise.
Model tenant-escape and cross-customer attacks.
Model automation, scraping, spam, fraud, and economic abuse.
Model recovery-system and backup attacks.
Model support-channel and account-recovery social engineering.
Convert identified threats into requirements and tests.
Revisit the threat model after material design or scope changes.
Obtain independent review for high-value or high-risk systems.
One authoritative source repository is identified.
Repository access uses individual identities rather than shared accounts.
Strong authentication is required for repository access.
Access follows least privilege.
Protected branches prevent unreviewed direct changes.
Material changes require independent review.
Critical code areas require designated reviewers.
Review cannot be bypassed silently by administrators.
Merge requirements include the required automated checks.
Security-sensitive changes receive appropriate specialist review.
Infrastructure, pipeline, authorization, cryptography, payment, and migration changes receive heightened review.
Changes are traceable from requirement or issue to code, review, build, artifact, and deployment.
Commit history and release tags are protected against unauthorized rewriting.
Secret scanning covers current changes and repository history.
Large binaries, generated files, and vendored code are controlled.
Generated code has a documented trusted source and regeneration process.
Emergency changes follow a documented break-glass process and receive retrospective review.
Repository backup and recovery have been tested.
Departed personnel and obsolete automation identities no longer have access.
Repository webhooks, apps, bots, and deploy keys are inventoried and restricted.
Builds run from reviewed source.
Builds are automated and repeatable.
A clean build produces equivalent output from the same declared inputs.
Build inputs and dependency versions are pinned sufficiently to prevent unexpected substitution.
Builds fail closed when required verification cannot run.
The production artifact is built once and promoted, not independently rebuilt in each environment.
Deployable artifacts are immutable.
Every artifact has a cryptographic digest.
Build provenance records source, builder, inputs, commands or workflow, time, and output digest.
Artifact signatures or attestations are verified before deployment.
Build identities and signing keys use least privilege.
Build and signing keys are stored outside source code and build output.
Build runners are patched and isolated appropriately.
Untrusted contribution workflows cannot access production secrets.
Pull-request builds cannot overwrite trusted release artifacts.
CI jobs have minimum required network, repository, cloud, and registry permissions.
Pipeline definitions receive the same review protection as application code.
Required unit, integration, security, policy, and packaging checks cannot be skipped silently.
Failed or canceled checks cannot be misrepresented as passed.
Artifact registries enforce authentication, authorization, immutability, and retention.
The previous known-good artifact remains available.
Build logs do not expose secrets or sensitive source material.
Build caches cannot substitute unverified or cross-trust artifacts.
Release tags, artifacts, provenance, and deployment records agree.
Compromise of the build platform has a documented containment and recovery procedure.
A supply-chain incident drill has tested revocation, rebuild, resigning, and redeployment.
Generate an SBOM for every released application artifact.
Include direct and transitive components.
Include runtime, operating-system, container, client, server, plugin, model, and embedded components as applicable.
Distinguish build-only, development-only, optional, and runtime dependencies.
Record exact versions, package identifiers, sources, hashes, and relationships.
Record license information and required notices.
Link the SBOM to the released artifact digest.
Verify the SBOM against the final packaged artifact.
Ensure no unexpected undeclared components are present.
Remove unused dependencies.
Remove unsupported and end-of-life dependencies.
Check whether dependencies come from intended publishers and registries.
Protect against dependency confusion, namespace collision, and typographical substitution.
Assess maintainer health and abandonment risk for critical dependencies.
Monitor upstream security advisories.
Continuously scan released components for newly disclosed vulnerabilities.
Prioritize vulnerabilities using exploit activity, reachability, exposure, asset criticality, data sensitivity, and compensating controls.
Check relevant known-exploited-vulnerability catalogs.
Define remediation targets by actual risk.
Verify fixes or mitigations after deployment.
Maintain a process for emergency replacement of a compromised dependency.
Document ownership of vendored, forked, or internally patched components.
Test updates before promotion.
Verify license compatibility among combined components.
Provide required attributions, source offers, notices, and redistribution terms.
Ensure proprietary or confidential code is not unintentionally incorporated into distributable artifacts.
Retain SBOMs for historical releases and incident investigation.
Development, testing, staging, and production are meaningfully separated.
Production credentials do not work in non-production environments.
Non-production users cannot reach production control planes.
Staging is sufficiently production-like to validate topology, integrations, migrations, and deployment behavior.
Production data is not copied to non-production without authorization and protection.
Test accounts, bypasses, simulators, and debug endpoints are absent or inaccessible in production.
Non-production email, payment, notifications, and webhooks cannot accidentally contact real users.
Environment boundaries are documented and tested.
Production access is logged and periodically reviewed.
Configuration is version-controlled or otherwise auditable.
Configuration changes require review and approval.
Configuration has schema and type validation.
Missing configuration fails safely rather than activating insecure defaults.
Secure defaults are used.
Environment-specific values are explicit.
Configuration drift is detected.
Production configuration can be reconstructed.
Configuration rollback is tested.
Debug mode, verbose exception output, profiling, test routes, and development consoles are disabled.
Time zones, locales, character encodings, and units are explicit.
Time synchronization is monitored.
Resource limits and timeouts are explicitly configured.
Production source maps and diagnostic artifacts do not expose secrets or inappropriate internal information.
Configuration ownership and expiration dates are recorded.
Emergency configuration changes are captured and reviewed.
Every flag has an owner.
Every flag has a documented purpose.
Default behavior is safe when the flag service fails.
Flag state is included in release and incident records.
Access to change high-impact flags is restricted and audited.
Flag combinations are tested.
A kill switch exists for high-risk new functionality where appropriate.
Flag changes can be rolled back quickly.
Temporary flags have removal dates.
Stale flags and dead code are removed.
Secrets are stored in an approved secret-management system.
No secrets exist in source, images, frontend bundles, logs, tickets, documentation, chat history, or analytics.
Secrets are unique across environments.
Each workload uses its own scoped identity or credential.
Credentials follow least privilege.
Short-lived credentials are preferred where supported.
Secret retrieval and use are audited.
Secret rotation has been tested.
Emergency revocation has been tested.
Credential expiry and rotation failures are monitored.
Old credentials are invalidated after rotation.
Backup and recovery procedures preserve or reconstruct necessary secrets securely.
Break-glass credentials are protected, monitored, and periodically tested.
No default or vendor-supplied credentials remain.
Suspected historical secret exposure has been addressed by rotation, not merely deletion from source.
Every requirement maps to at least one verification activity.
Every critical user journey passes end to end.
Positive, negative, boundary, and invalid-input cases pass.
Empty-state behavior is correct.
Maximum-size and high-volume behavior is correct.
Duplicate submissions do not create unintended duplicate effects.
Refresh, retry, browser navigation, and network interruption do not corrupt state.
Concurrent requests do not violate business invariants.
Race conditions have been tested around balances, inventory, permissions, limits, and state transitions.
State transitions reject invalid orderings.
Operations that must be idempotent are demonstrably idempotent.
Partial failures cannot leave an ambiguous or silently inconsistent result.
Transactions are atomic where required.
Eventually consistent operations expose correct pending and completion states.
Reconciliation detects missing, duplicated, or mismatched records.
Numeric precision and rounding are correct.
Money calculations use correct decimal, currency, tax, and rounding rules.
Time calculations handle time zones, daylight-saving changes, leap years, month boundaries, and clock differences.
Unicode, normalization, collation, and case behavior do not create duplicates or bypasses.
Limits and quotas are enforced server-side.
Approval and four-eyes workflows cannot be bypassed.
Cancellation, refund, reversal, deletion, and undo operations are complete.
Account suspension and termination affect every relevant session, token, worker, and integration.
Import and export behavior is complete and validated.
Long-running operations can resume safely or fail clearly.
Scheduled jobs handle missed runs, overlapping runs, retries, and duplicate execution.
Background jobs preserve user, authorization, and tenant context.
Dead-lettered operations can be inspected and replayed safely.
Administrative actions produce the intended effect and audit trail.
Support tools cannot create states impossible through the normal product.
Failure defaults to the safer state.
Error messages tell users what they can do next without exposing sensitive details.
Known limitations are documented accurately.
A documented test strategy exists for the release risk level.
Tests cover unit, component, integration, contract, system, end-to-end, smoke, and regression levels as appropriate.
Tests prioritize critical and high-risk behavior rather than relying solely on aggregate coverage.
Coverage gaps in critical code are explicitly reviewed.
Test data is representative of real size, shape, encoding, and edge conditions.
Personal or confidential test data is synthetic, masked, or properly authorized.
Tests are deterministic enough to act as release gates.
Flaky gating tests are fixed or formally quarantined with risk review.
Test failures cannot be dismissed without evidence.
Tests validate failure and recovery, not only successful operation.
Contract tests cover internal and external interfaces.
Compatibility tests cover supported clients and versions.
Migration, upgrade, mixed-version, downgrade, rollback, and roll-forward scenarios are tested.
Performance tests cover load, stress, spike, endurance, and capacity limits.
Resilience tests inject relevant dependency, network, storage, and resource failures.
Security testing covers source, dependencies, deployed behavior, infrastructure, configuration, and business logic.
Accessibility testing combines automation with manual keyboard and assistive-technology checks.
Property-based, fuzz, mutation, model-based, or combinatorial testing is used for high-risk parsers and stateful logic where useful.
Critical calculations use independent test or reconciliation methods.
Tests run against production-like topology and configuration.
Tests verify the actual artifact intended for production.
Evidence identifies test version, data, environment, build, and result.
Failed tests are linked to fixes and successful retests.
Material changes trigger the relevant regression suite.
Independent user acceptance is complete.
An independent penetration test is completed where risk, contract, or regulation warrants it.
Testing limitations and untested conditions are disclosed in the readiness decision.
A supported browser and device matrix is documented.
Unsupported clients receive reasonable behavior or a clear message.
Critical journeys work on every supported browser.
Layout works at supported viewport sizes.
Portrait and landscape behavior is correct where relevant.
Zoom and text enlargement do not hide essential functionality.
Touch, mouse, keyboard, and assistive input work appropriately.
Loading, empty, success, warning, error, partial, timeout, and offline states are designed.
Forms preserve appropriate input after recoverable errors.
Validation is understandable and points to the affected field.
Back, forward, refresh, bookmarks, and deep links behave correctly.
Multiple tabs and windows do not corrupt session or workflow state.
Client-side caching does not expose another user’s data.
Browser storage contains no unnecessary sensitive data.
Logout and account deletion clear appropriate client state.
Client-side authorization is never treated as the security boundary.
Client-side execution being unavailable or failing degrades acceptably where required.
Third-party script failure does not break critical operation unnecessarily.
No unhandled exceptions or material console errors remain.
Source maps, diagnostic data, and stack traces are appropriately restricted.
Error pages do not expose internals.
Download, print, copy, paste, and upload behaviors work where supported.
Long text, translated text, unusual names, and bidirectional text are handled.
Destructive operations require suitable confirmation or reversal.
Navigation and controls are consistent.
Users are not trapped in dead ends.
Session timeout warnings and recovery preserve work where appropriate.
Autosave behavior is transparent and reliable.
User feedback is not lost during asynchronous operations.
Client and server validation produce consistent outcomes.
Analytics and experimentation code do not alter critical behavior.
Dark patterns, deceptive defaults, and misleading urgency are absent.
The required WCAG version and conformance level are documented.
Automated accessibility scans pass within the accepted threshold.
Critical journeys have been tested manually using only a keyboard.
No keyboard trap exists.
Focus order follows a meaningful sequence.
Focus is visibly indicated.
Focus is not obscured by sticky headers, dialogs, banners, or overlays.
Page titles, headings, landmarks, regions, and lists use meaningful semantics.
Every interactive control has an accessible name, role, state, and value.
Custom controls expose equivalent semantics and keyboard behavior.
Images have appropriate alternative text or are correctly marked decorative.
Audio and video have required captions, transcripts, and descriptions.
Information is not communicated by color alone.
Text and meaningful visual elements meet contrast requirements.
Content reflows and remains usable when zoomed.
Text spacing changes do not break content.
Touch and pointer targets are sufficiently usable.
Dragging has a non-drag alternative where required.
Motion, animation, autoplay, and flashing are controlled safely.
“Reduce motion” or equivalent preferences are respected where relevant.
Forms have explicit labels and understandable instructions.
Required fields and formats are conveyed accessibly.
Errors are identified, described, and associated with fields.
Error summaries and status changes are announced to assistive technologies.
Authentication does not rely solely on inaccessible puzzles or memory tests.
Time limits can be extended or disabled where required.
Repeated entry of the same information is minimized.
Help is located consistently.
Language and text direction are declared correctly.
Tables expose proper headers and relationships.
Dialogs, menus, tabs, tooltips, and notifications follow accessible interaction patterns.
Dynamic content changes are announced appropriately.
Downloaded documents are accessible.
Third-party embedded components meet the required level or have an accessible alternative.
Testing includes representative screen-reader combinations.
Testing includes users with disabilities where the product’s impact warrants it.
An accessibility statement and issue-reporting path exist.
Accessibility defects have owners, severity, and remediation dates.
Accessibility remains part of regression testing after launch.
Maintain a complete API inventory.
Every API has an owner and documented consumers.
Interface schemas and behavior are versioned.
Authentication is enforced on every protected operation.
Authorization is evaluated for every object, property, operation, and tenant.
Input is validated against an explicit schema.
Unknown or prohibited fields are rejected or handled safely.
Content types and character encodings are constrained.
Request body, URL, header, nesting, field, query, and batch sizes are bounded.
Expensive queries and filters have cost controls.
Pagination has safe maximums.
Sorting and filtering cannot bypass access control.
Mass assignment and unexpected property binding are prevented.
HTTP methods have correct and consistent semantics.
Idempotency is implemented where retries can repeat effects.
Concurrency control prevents lost updates where required.
Timeouts exist for all outbound calls.
Retries are bounded and use backoff and jitter.
Retries occur only for safe or idempotent operations.
Circuit breaking or equivalent isolation exists for unstable dependencies.
Errors use consistent safe structures and appropriate status codes.
Error responses do not expose stack traces, queries, secrets, or internal topology.
Rate limits and quotas protect users, tenants, infrastructure, and dependencies.
Rate limits cannot be trivially bypassed through alternate identifiers or routes.
CORS uses explicit trusted origins where cross-origin access is needed.
Credentialed cross-origin requests do not use wildcard origins.
Browser-authenticated state-changing operations have CSRF protection.
Sensitive credentials and tokens never appear in URLs.
Redirects and callback destinations are strictly validated.
Server-side outbound destinations are constrained to prevent SSRF.
URL parsing is consistent across proxies, application code, and security controls.
Host-header and forwarded-header trust is explicitly configured.
Request smuggling, response splitting, cache poisoning, and parser ambiguity have been assessed.
Webhooks are authenticated or signed.
Webhooks include replay protection.
Webhook consumers are idempotent.
Webhook retries, ordering, failure, and reconciliation are defined.
API keys are scoped, rotated, revocable, and attributable.
Secrets are not returned in responses or documentation examples.
Backward compatibility is tested.
Breaking-change and deprecation policies exist.
Old versions have retirement dates and monitoring.
Contract tests cover external providers and consumers.
API documentation matches deployed behavior.
Production examples contain no real credentials or personal data.
Graph-based APIs limit depth, breadth, recursion, aliases, batching, and computational cost.
Graph schema introspection exposure is intentionally decided.
WebSocket or streaming connections authenticate securely.
Streaming connections verify origin where browser initiated.
Authorization changes and logout invalidate long-lived connections.
Reconnect, ordering, deduplication, backpressure, and heartbeat behavior are tested.
File-transfer APIs apply the file-security controls in this checklist.
Partner and machine-to-machine APIs use appropriately scoped identities.
Public APIs have abuse controls, usage policies, and security contact information.
Inventory every login, enrollment, recovery, federation, API, support, and administrative authentication path.
Select identity and authentication assurance appropriate to the harm of account compromise.
Require stronger authentication for privileged and high-impact accounts.
Support phishing-resistant authentication where risk warrants it.
Multifactor enrollment is protected from account takeover.
New authenticators require appropriate reauthentication.
Removing or replacing an authenticator requires appropriate verification.
Password handling follows current guidance.
Passwords are not silently truncated or transformed unexpectedly.
Common and compromised passwords are rejected where password authentication is used.
Password managers and paste are supported.
Login defenses address credential stuffing and brute force.
Defenses avoid creating trivial denial-of-service against legitimate users.
Login, registration, and recovery responses do not unnecessarily disclose whether an account exists.
Account enrollment verifies the correct communication channel or identity evidence.
Account recovery is no weaker than normal authentication.
Recovery cannot be redirected through an unverified channel.
Recovery tokens are single-use, short-lived, random, and stored safely.
Password or authenticator reset invalidates appropriate sessions and recovery material.
High-risk operations require recent authentication.
Email, phone, payout, identity, and security-setting changes notify the user appropriately.
Changes to recovery information use delayed or additional verification where warranted.
Default credentials are absent.
Test, dormant, abandoned, and terminated accounts are disabled.
Service accounts cannot use interactive recovery mechanisms inappropriately.
Authentication events are audited.
Suspicious authentication can trigger step-up controls or investigation.
Users can review and revoke relevant sessions and devices.
Clock skew and token timing behavior are tested.
Recovery codes are protected, single-use, and regenerated securely.
Support personnel cannot bypass identity checks without a controlled, audited exception process.
Social-engineering resistance is included in support procedures.
Issuer, audience, signature, algorithm, expiration, nonce, and state are validated.
Redirect URIs are matched exactly according to the protocol’s security requirements.
Authorization-code flows use current protections such as proof-key mechanisms where applicable.
Deprecated or insecure delegated-authorization flows are not used.
Token substitution and mix-up attacks are addressed.
Identity-provider accounts are linked only after secure verification.
Automatic account linking cannot merge an attacker’s identity with a victim’s account.
Tokens are scoped to the minimum required audience and permissions.
Access and refresh tokens are stored and transmitted safely.
Refresh-token rotation and reuse detection are applied where appropriate.
Revocation, logout, key rotation, and identity-provider outage behavior are tested.
Federation metadata and signing keys are refreshed safely.
Identity claims are not trusted beyond their documented assurance.
Tenant or organization selection cannot be manipulated to cross boundaries.
Authorization is denied by default.
Authorization is enforced server-side at every trusted boundary.
A current role-permission-resource matrix exists.
Every endpoint and action maps to a required permission.
Access checks use the current user, tenant, resource, and operation.
Object ownership is verified on every direct and indirect object reference.
Horizontal privilege escalation has been tested.
Vertical privilege escalation has been tested.
Function-level and property-level authorization have been tested.
Bulk, export, search, reporting, and aggregation endpoints enforce the same controls as individual records.
Hidden fields and client-side controls cannot grant access.
Role changes take effect promptly across sessions, caches, queues, and services.
Removed users lose access to shared resources.
Nested groups and inherited permissions are tested.
Temporary permissions expire automatically.
Privileged access follows least privilege and just-in-time principles where practical.
High-impact actions require additional approval where appropriate.
Administrative, support, and impersonation actions require reason, authorization, visible indication, and audit.
Impersonation never exposes secrets the support user should not receive.
Emergency access is time-bounded and reviewed.
Authorization decisions are logged at an appropriate level.
Background jobs retain correct authorization and tenant context.
Caches do not return data authorized for another principal.
Search indexes preserve authorization boundaries.
Files, exports, backups, logs, and analytics preserve tenant boundaries.
Queue messages cannot be reassigned across tenants through manipulated metadata.
Tenant-specific encryption, keys, domains, and configuration are isolated as designed.
Resource identifiers alone are never treated as authorization.
Side channels do not disclose another tenant’s existence, activity, identifiers, or resource usage.
Automated tests cover every role × operation × resource-state combination considered material.
Session identifiers have sufficient unpredictability.
Session identifiers are generated using a cryptographically secure source.
Session identifiers are never accepted from insecure or unintended channels.
Browser cookies use `Secure` where transmitted over HTTPS.
Sensitive browser cookies use `HttpOnly` unless script access is essential and justified.
`SameSite` behavior is intentionally selected and tested.
Cookie domain and path scope are as narrow as practical.
Cross-subdomain cookie trust is explicitly assessed.
Session identifiers rotate after login and privilege changes.
Session fixation is prevented.
Idle and absolute timeouts match risk and user needs.
Logout invalidates the server-side session or otherwise revokes access.
Account recovery and credential change invalidate appropriate sessions.
Concurrent-session policy is defined.
Users can identify and revoke sessions where appropriate.
“Remember me” behavior has separate, appropriately constrained credentials.
Sensitive state-changing actions have CSRF protection.
Tokens validate issuer, audience, subject, type, signature, algorithm, expiry, and not-before values.
A token intended for one purpose cannot be accepted for another.
Token replay risk is addressed.
Refresh credentials are rotated or otherwise protected against replay where appropriate.
Tokens and session identifiers are absent from URLs, referrers, analytics, logs, and error reports.
Client-side storage of tokens is minimized and threat-modeled.
Logout, revocation, and compromise behavior is tested across all application components.
Session-related logs do not expose reusable credentials.
All untrusted input is identified.
Validation occurs at the trusted server-side boundary.
Inputs are validated for type, syntax, range, length, structure, and allowed values.
Canonicalization and normalization occur before security-sensitive comparisons.
Validation uses allowlists where a finite valid set exists.
Database operations use safe parameter binding.
Operating-system operations avoid command construction from untrusted input.
Directory, query, search, template, expression, mail, logging, and interpreter contexts use appropriate safe APIs.
Output is encoded for its exact destination context.
HTML or rich-text content is sanitized with an appropriate maintained sanitizer.
Untrusted input cannot escape into executable script, style, markup, query, command, or template contexts.
Dynamic evaluation of untrusted input is absent.
Unsafe deserialization is avoided.
Deserialization permits only expected types and bounded structures.
XML processing disables unnecessary external entity and external resource behavior.
Path traversal and archive traversal are prevented.
Symbolic-link and filesystem race behavior is controlled.
Server-side request forgery protections constrain protocol, destination, redirects, DNS resolution, and metadata endpoints.
Regular expressions cannot be used for practical resource-exhaustion attacks.
Header, response-splitting, log, CSV, formula, and email injection are addressed.
Open redirects are prevented.
Object and property injection through automatic binding or merge behavior is addressed.
Unicode confusables and normalization do not bypass validation or identity checks.
Error handling does not reflect unsafe input into executable contexts.
Security tests cover injection across every supported parser and protocol.
File upload is enabled only where necessary.
Maximum file size is enforced before excessive processing.
File count, archive depth, expanded size, dimensions, page count, and processing time are bounded.
File type is checked using content, structure, and expected extension rather than user-supplied metadata alone.
Allowed types are explicitly listed.
Active or executable content is rejected or neutralized where not required.
Uploaded content is malware-scanned where risk warrants it.
Files remain quarantined until required validation completes.
User-provided filenames are not used as trusted filesystem paths.
Stored filenames are non-predictable where guessing would create risk.
Upload storage is non-executable.
Untrusted files use an isolated origin where browser execution could be dangerous.
